desc:
Delete as few elements as possible from nums so that no two different values that remain occur the same number of times. (A value that disappears completely no longer counts.)

Return the minimum number of deletions.

For example, [1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3] gives 3: the three values all occur twice, so reduce them to frequencies 2, 1 and 0 by deleting 0 + 1 + 2 elements.
hints: Only the frequency of each value matters. Work with the list of frequencies, not the array.
If two values have the same frequency, one of them must lose at least one element. Lowering a frequency by one costs exactly one deletion.

Process frequencies from the largest to the smallest. Keep the highest frequency limit that is still allowed: each value takes min(freq, limit) and then the limit drops by one (but not below zero). Sum the differences.
editorial: Collect the frequencies of the distinct values and sort them in descending order, or bucket them by size: cc[f] is the number of values that have frequency f. Scan f from the maximum down to 1 carrying extra, the number of values that are stuck on a taken frequency. At each f, total = cc[f] + extra; one value may keep f, so extra = total - 1 (if total > 0), and each of those extra values pays one deletion to step down to f - 1.

Equivalently, in the sorted view each value takes the largest frequency not exceeding its own that is still free. A frequency may drop all the way to zero, in which case the value is deleted entirely and its slot is no longer blocking anyone. The total work is O(n) with the bucket scan, or O(d log d) with sorting.
